extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, and appellants before the Board of Patent Appeals & Interferences (BPAI)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal principles applied by the BPAI in an appeal evaluating 35 U.S.C. § 101 (patentable subject matter) and § 103 (obviousness), particularly for software/Beauregard-type claims. Covers claim construction, prior-art comparison, and procedural rules on appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on appellant to demonstrate error
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellant has the burden on appeal to the Board to demonstrate error in the Examiner's position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: In re Kahn (441 F.3d 977) — an appellant can overcome a rejection by showing insufficient evidence of prima facie obviousness or rebutting the prima facie case with evidence (e.g., secondary indicia). The Board will affirm where appellant fails to meet this burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step inquiry for anticipation and obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "[B]oth anticipation under §102 and obviousness under §103 are two-step inquiries. The first step in both analyses is a proper construction of the claims ... The second step in the analyses requires a comparison of the properly construed claim to the prior art." (Medichem v. Rolabo cited)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction must be performed before comparing claim scope to the prior art; errors in either step can determine the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims interpreted as broadly as their terms reasonably allow
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be interpreted as broadly as their terms reasonably allow. (In re Zletz, 893 F.2d 319, 321)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board follows the principle that claim terms are given their ordinary meaning unless the specification fixes a special definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: "The words of a claim 'are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning.' ... The 'ordinary and customary meaning of a claim term is the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art ... as of the effective filing date." (Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless the specification discloses a special definition, the common meaning is used in claim construction and in comparing to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject matter: laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, physical phenomena and abstract ideas are excluded from patent protection. (Diamond v. Diehr)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a claim is directed to any of these excluded categories when assessing §101; an otherwise useful application may still fail if it's only an abstract idea without an inventive application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Useful, concrete and tangible result test (State Street) is inadequate post-Bilski
rubrics_metrics.description: The test for statutory subject matter as whether it is a 'practical application,' i.e., produces 'a useful, concrete and tangible result' (State Street) is no longer dispositive after In re Bilski.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portions of opinions relying solely on 'useful, concrete and tangible result' should not be relied on; Bilski limits reliance on State Street for §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test is the proper test to apply (post-Bilski)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We also conclude that the 'useful, concrete and tangible result' inquiry is inadequate and reaffirm that the machine-or-transformation test outlines by the Supreme Court is the proper test to apply." (In re Bilski paraphrase in decision)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the machine-or-transformation framework to assess whether an asserted process is patent-eligible under §101 (i.e., tied to a particular machine or transforms an article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauregard claims considered statutory at the USPTO (MPEP 2105.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been the practice for a number of years that a 'Beauregard Claim' of this nature be considered statutory at the USPTO as a product claim. (MPEP 2105.01, I)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not finally adjudicated by the Federal Circuit, the USPTO practice treats computer-readable-medium claims containing program code as statutory, consistent with certain precedent (e.g., In re Lowry).

rubrics_metrics.name: In re Nuijten: consider statutory classes for signals
rubrics_metrics.description: In the analysis of In re Nuijten, the Federal Circuit considers the four statutory classes for a signal, and bases determination of statutory subject matter on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims involve transitory signals or similar matter, consider the statutory class analysis from Nuijten in assessing §101 issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of software components embodied on a computer-readable medium can be statutory (In re Lowry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of software components embodied upon a computer readable medium has been found statutory under the teachings of In re Lowry, 32 F.3d 1579 (Fed. Cir., 1994).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precedent supports the view that a claimed combination of modules on a medium may satisfy §101 where the claims recite tangible embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR common-sense teaching for obviousness (combining familiar items)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is common sense that familiar items may have obvious uses beyond their primary purposes, and a person of ordinary skill often will be able to fit the teachings of multiple patents together like pieces of a puzzle." (KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex, Inc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For §103 obviousness, courts may rely on common sense and the obviousness of combining known elements if a skilled artisan would find it predictable to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must present a prima facie case; applicant may rebut
rubrics_metrics.description: The record supports the following findings ... The Examiner has presented a prima facie case for the rejections of Appellant's claims under 35 U.S.C. §§101 and 103. ... On appeal to the Board, an applicant can overcome a rejection by showing insufficient evidence of prima facie obviousness or by rebutting the prima facie case with evidence of secondary indicia of nonobviousness. (Kahn; Rouffet cited)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Examiner presents a prima facie case, the applicant must present evidence or arguments (including secondary considerations) to rebut that case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim practice when briefs deficient (37 CFR / McDaniel)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the brief fails to meet either requirement [of 37 CFR §1.192(c)(7)], the Board is free to select a single claim from each group of claims subject to a common ground of rejection as representative ... and to decide the appeal ... based solely on the selected representative claim. (In re McDaniel)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedurally, the Board may pick a representative claim and treat it as dispositive for a group of claims when appellants' briefing does not adequately address each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments not raised are waived
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those arguments actually made by Appellant have been considered in this opinion. Arguments which Appellant could have made but chose not to make in the Briefs have not been considered and are deemed to be waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellants must present arguments in their briefs to preserve them for Board consideration; failure to do so forfeits those arguments on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming/labeling functional modules does not negate obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The naming of a module by certain nomenclature, for example 'configuration file processing module', does not render the module structurally or functionally unobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely reciting module names or labels in claims is insufficient to show nonobviousness if the underlying functionality is taught or obvious in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-meaning of technical terms can be relied upon absent special definition
rubrics_metrics.description: We find the common meaning of the word, absent any special and express definition in the Specification, to be suggested by Shaughnessy. (See Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and the Board may apply the ordinary technical meaning of claim terms unless the specification supplies a special definition; do not rely on idiosyncratic gloss without specification support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural: no time extension under 37 C.F.R. §1.136(a)(1)(iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: No time period for taking any subsequent action in connection with this appeal may be extended under 37 C.F.R. §1.136(a). See 37 C.F.R. §1.136(a)(1)(iv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After issuance of the decision, statutory deadlines for further action in connection with the appeal are not extendable under the cited regulation.
